subtopic: Enthalpies for Different Types of Reactions
stem: The combustion of one mole of benzene takes place at \(298\,\text{K}\) and \(1\,\text{atm}\). After combustion, \(\text{CO}_2(g)\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) are produced and \(3267.0\,\text{kJ}\) of heat is liberated. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation, \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) of benzene. Standard enthalpies of formation of \(\text{CO}_2(g)\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) are \(-393.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(-285.83\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) respectively.
solution:
[Textbook error in this worked example, CORRECTED below rather than preserved, because a printed worked solution is a method a student copies. The book reverses equation (ii) to obtain (vi) but keeps its enthalpy NEGATIVE, at \(-3267.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); reversing a reaction must flip the sign. The defect is self-refuting on the book's own arithmetic: adding its printed (v) and (vi) as printed gives \(-3218.49 + (-3267.0) = -6485.49\), not the \(-48.51\) it goes on to print — while \(-3218.49 + 3267.0 = +48.51\) exactly, so the book evidently computed with \(+3267.0\) and then printed the sign wrong a second time on its final line. Corroborated independently by the book itself: Table 5.2 lists the standard enthalpy of formation of benzene(l) as \(+49.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Benzene is an endothermic compound, so a NEGATIVE \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) is not merely a slip of sign but the opposite chemical claim. Two further defects are left as printed because they change nothing: the reversed equation is still labelled \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) where \(-\Delta_C H^{\ominus}\) belongs, and the final line re-uses the label "(iv)", already used by equation (iv) above it.] The formation reaction of benzene is given by:
\(6\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6(l)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = ?\) … (i)
The enthalpy of combustion of 1 mol of benzene is:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6(l) + \dfrac{15}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\); \(\Delta_C H^{\ominus} = -3267\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) … (ii)
The enthalpy of formation of 1 mol of \(\text{CO}_2(g)\):
\(\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = -393.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) … (iii)
The enthalpy of formation of 1 mol of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) is:
\(\text{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\); \(\Delta_C H^{\ominus} = -285.83\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) … (iv)
Multiplying eqn. (iii) by 6 and eqn. (iv) by 3 we get:
\(6\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + 6\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2(g)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = -2361\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(3\text{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{3}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = -857.49\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Summing up the above two equations:
\(6\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + 3\text{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{15}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = -3218.49\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) … (v)
Reversing equation (ii);
\(6\text{CO}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6(l) + \dfrac{15}{2}\text{O}_2\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = +3267.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) … (vi)
Adding equations (v) and (vi), we get
\(6\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6(l)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = +48.51\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) … (iv)
_note: Transcribed exactly as printed; the printed solution carries FOUR defects. (1) Eqn (vi) is the REVERSE of (ii), so its enthalpy must be \(+3267.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), not \(-3267.0\). (2) Consequently the final answer is \(-3218.49 + 3267.0 = +48.51\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), not \(-48.51\) — and the book's own Table 5.2 (p.149) lists \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6, l) = +49.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), confirming the sign. (3) The final line is labelled '(iv)', re-using the label already given to the \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) formation step; it should be (vii). (4) Steps (iv) and (vi) are labelled \(\Delta_C H^{\ominus}\) / \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}\) inconsistently with what they describe (a formation and a reverse-combustion respectively). Needs maintainer adjudication.

stem:
Predict in which of the following, entropy increases/decreases:
(i) A liquid crystallizes into a solid.
(ii) Temperature of a crystalline solid is raised from \(0\,\text{K}\) to \(115\,\text{K}\).
(iii) \(2\text{NaHCO}_3(s) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\)
(iv) \(\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}(g)\)
solution:
(i) After freezing, the molecules attain an ordered state and therefore, entropy decreases.
(ii) At \(0\,\text{K}\), the constituent particles are static and entropy is minimum. If temperature is raised to \(115\,\text{K}\), these begin to move and oscillate about their equilibrium positions in the lattice and system becomes more disordered, therefore entropy increases.
(iii) Reactant, \(\text{NaHCO}_3\) is a solid and it has low entropy. Among products there are one solid and two gases. Therefore, the products represent a condition of higher entropy.
(iv) Here one molecule gives two atoms i.e., number of particles increases leading to more disordered state. Two moles of H atoms have higher entropy than one mole of dihydrogen molecule.
_note: The book prints 'contituent' for 'constituent' in part (ii); transcribed with the spelling corrected.

stem:
For oxidation of iron,
\(4\text{Fe}(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3(s)\)
entropy change is \(-549.4\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) at \(298\,\text{K}\). Inspite of negative entropy change of this reaction, why is the reaction spontaneous?
(\(\Delta_r H^{\ominus}\) for this reaction is \(-1648 \times 10^{3}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\))
solution:
One decides the spontaneity of a reaction by considering \(\Delta S_{total}\,(\Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr})\). For calculating \(\Delta S_{surr}\), we have to consider the heat absorbed by the surroundings which is equal to \(-\Delta_r H^{\ominus}\). At temperature \(T\), entropy change of the surroundings is
\(\Delta S_{surr} = -\dfrac{\Delta_r H^{\ominus}}{T}\) (at constant pressure)
\(= -\dfrac{(-1648 \times 10^{3}\,\text{J mol}^{-1})}{298\,\text{K}} = 5530\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Thus, total entropy change for this reaction
\(\Delta_r S_{total} = 5530\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} + (-549.4\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}) = 4980.6\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\)
This shows that the above reaction is spontaneous.

stem: Calculate \(\Delta_r G^{\ominus}\) for conversion of oxygen to ozone, \(\dfrac{3}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{O}_3(g)\) at \(298\,\text{K}\), if \(K_p\) for this conversion is \(2.47 \times 10^{-29}\).
solution:
We know \(\Delta_r G^{\ominus} = -2.303\,\text{R}T \log K_p\) and \(\text{R} = 8.314\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\)
Therefore, \(\Delta_r G^{\ominus} = -2.303\,(8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}) \times (298\,\text{K})\,(\log 2.47 \times 10^{-29})\)
\(= 163000\,\text{J mol}^{-1} = 163\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

stem:
Find out the value of equilibrium constant for the following reaction at \(298\,\text{K}\).
\(2\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_2\text{CONH}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)
Standard Gibbs energy change, \(\Delta_r G^{\ominus}\) at the given temperature is \(-13.6\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).
At \(60\,^\circ\text{C}\), dinitrogen tetroxide is 50 per cent dissociated. Calculate the standard free energy change at this temperature and at one atmosphere.
solution:
[Textbook errors in this worked example. TWO defects, treated differently on purpose. (1) THE UNIT IS CORRECTED. The printed line multiplies \(\text{R} = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) by a temperature and two dimensionless factors, so the result is JOULES per mole; the book prints \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), overstating the free-energy change by a factor of 1000. That is unambiguous and is fixed below. (2) THE VALUE IS LEFT AS PRINTED AND IS FLAGGED RATHER THAN CHANGED. Evaluating the book's own printed factors, \(8.314 \times 333 \times 2.303 \times 0.1239 = 790.0\), so the line does not give the \(763.8\) it prints. We cannot reconstruct which of the book's inputs it actually intended — no self-consistent reading of \(K_p\), \(T\) or \(\log K_p\) reproduces 763.8 — and inventing a correction would be worse than naming a defect, so the printed value stands. Expect the book's \(-763.8\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\) in any answer key; a derivation from the stated data gives about \(-790\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\).] \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)\)
If \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\) is 50% dissociated, the mole fraction of both the substances is given by
\(x_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} = \dfrac{1 - 0.5}{1 + 0.5}\); \(x_{\text{NO}_2} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.5}{1 + 0.5}\)
\(p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.5} \times 1\,\text{atm}\), \(p_{\text{NO}_2} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} \times 1\,\text{atm}\)
The equilibrium constant \(K_p\) is given by
\(K_p = \dfrac{(p_{\text{NO}_2})^{2}}{p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4}} = \dfrac{1.5}{(1.5)^{2}(0.5)} = 1.33\,\text{atm}\)
Since \(\Delta_r G^{\ominus} = -\text{R}T \ln K_p\)
\(\Delta_r G^{\ominus} = (-8.314\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}) \times (333\,\text{K}) \times (2.303) \times (0.1239)\)
\(= -763.8\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)
_note: Transcribed as printed. Two defects in the printed solution: (1) the final UNIT is wrong — the product \((8.314)(333)(2.303)(0.1239)\) is in \(\text{J mol}^{-1}\), so the answer is of order \(-0.79\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), not \(-763.8\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); (2) the arithmetic itself gives \(-790\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\) rather than \(-763.8\). Needs maintainer adjudication.
